Covers the work since v1.1.37: the dashboard can now act on a gap instead of only
reporting one, and destructive actions can no longer be triggered anonymously or
by accident.

## Missing episodes can be downloaded

The coverage report has been able to tell you an episode was missing for a while,
but the chip was an inert `<span>` — the one status that most needs an action had
no way to trigger one. Missing chips are buttons now, and each arc header has a
**Download missing (N)** action that queues the whole arc in one request.

The real cause was upstream of the UI. `hasMagnet` was only computed for
`upgradeable` rows, so every missing episode reported `hasMagnet: false` no matter
what the feed actually held, and the modal always fell through to a manual search.
That is now computed for missing rows too, which is what makes the button worth
pressing.

`upgrade` turned out to be the only episode action that resolves a magnet with no
existing pipeline row, so it is the download path for an episode that isn't
tracked at all. It now says "Download started" rather than "Upgrade started" when
there was nothing on disk to replace.

## Destructive actions record who triggered them

A bulk removal of ~92 episodes left the log with no record of what had triggered
it — only what the effect was. Global actions, bulk episode actions (with the
target list and the delete-files flag), download-missing, and single removals now
log the requesting client before they act.

This paid for itself immediately: when 8 `done` rows disappeared from the live
pipeline right after deploying 1.1.39, the audit trail identified the exact
browser that cleared them, instead of it being indistinguishable from data loss
during an upgrade.

## Large file-deleting batches require a typed confirmation

Select-all plus one click was enough to delete the media files behind a large
selection, with no undo, and the modal's scrolling list had stopped conveying the
blast radius. Selections of five or more with "delete the media file" ticked now
require typing `DELETE` before the button enables. Small batches and file-keeping
removals are unchanged.

## Multi-select and sortable columns

Rows can be selected individually, with shift-click for a range or the header
checkbox for everything. A selection opens bulk **Retry** and **Remove** in the
card header, carrying over the single-episode dialog's "also delete the file"
option and listing what is about to go.

Every column header is now a sort button with `aria-sort` set. Resolution sorts
numerically (1080p above 720p, not as a string) and status sorts by pipeline
progression rather than alphabetically. Rows with no value sink to the bottom in
both directions rather than crowding the top.

Bulk work runs under a **single** acquisition of the action lock. The lock is a
plain boolean rather than reentrant, so looping the existing per-episode action
would have failed from the second episode on with
`Busy: "Retry episodes" is already running` — re-queuing exactly one download and
reporting the rest as errors. A failure on one episode no longer abandons the
batch: results are collected per episode and reported as a split ("Re-queued 2 of
3 — 1 failed"), with coverage refreshed once at the end rather than per episode.

## Resolution now outranks recency in the downgrade guard

One Pace re-encodes an arc at a lower resolution and republishes it, so the newest
release for a slot is regularly the *softer* one. The downgrade guard decided
purely on CRC32 catalog membership — an uncatalogued hash means "landed after the
dataset regenerated", i.e. newer — which carries no resolution signal at all. A
fresh 480p encode therefore replaced the 1080p file already in the library, and it
did so twice: Arlong Park S06E09 (480p `EB1B1AA6` over 1080p `0510B910`) and S06E07
(480p `AE7B08F2` over 1080p `4DDEFE2B`).

The guard now compares the incoming resolution tag against the on-disk one first:
softer is refused outright, sharper is allowed through, and only an equal or
missing tag falls back to the CRC32 recency rule — which still governs the
same-resolution re-release case it was written for, such as Wano S35E12. An
untagged file gives no signal and keeps the old behaviour, so natively-480p arcs
like Loguetown are unaffected.

The coverage report had the same blind spot in both directions: a 480p downgrade
on disk hid the canonical 1080p release behind "present (not in catalog yet)", so
the dashboard offered no way to recover, and it could offer a softer release as an
upgrade over a sharper file. It compares resolution before catalog membership too.

## Upgrading

Pull the new image and recreate the container. Nothing needs migrating — schema
changes are additive, and existing pipeline rows are untouched.
